source.title: Regularizers to the rescue: fighting overfitting in deep learning-based side-channel analysis

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; some figures are present only as plots.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies regularization techniques to deep-learning side-channel analysis and reports effects on held-out attack performance, extending regularization findings to a different task. It does not measure the training–test error gap named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports attack-phase guessing entropy (GE) and required attack traces (NT), not held-out classification error or the training–test error gap. Table 4 gives deterioration rates; figures report aggregate GE and NT comparisons without underlying numeric values. Profiling-time results do not bear on the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures regularization effects on side-channel key recovery using guessing entropy and required attack traces. These aggregate key-ranking outcomes do not measure the held-out classification error named by V6. Its CNN–MLP comparisons concern electromagnetic traces, not images as specified by V3. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the conclusion: L1 and L2 are the most effective tested regularizers by aggregate key-recovery performance and deterioration rate; early stopping has moderate effectiveness and reduces training time; dropout requires caution because deterioration is comparatively frequent and training time increases.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares explicitly regularized side-channel classifiers with unregularized baselines, using attack-phase key-ranking metrics rather than classification test error or the training–test gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset, leakage model and network topology. The paper reports higher deterioration rates for ID leakage settings and states that regularization effectiveness depends on dataset noise, leakage model and topology.

fits_no_version.finding: L1 and L2 generally improve key-recovery metrics, with deterioration rates of 0–6.5% and 0–2%, respectively. Dropout deterioration ranges from 7.5% to 29.5%; its mean guessing entropy worsens for ASCAD CNN-HW and MLP-ID even while mean required traces decrease.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In profiled side-channel analysis, tuned regularization affects aggregate key recovery differently across metrics, architectures, and leakage models; L1 and L2 are more reliable than dropout in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Among 500 randomly sampled ASCAD-HW models per architecture, 172 MLPs versus 70 CNNs reach GE=1; the five best CNNs need about 50 attack traces versus 550 for the five best MLPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this side-channel workload and search space, MLPs more often recover the key, while the best CNNs recover it with fewer traces.

record.problems: The reported outcomes are side-channel key-recovery metrics, not test error or a direct training–test gap. Aggregate GE and NT comparisons are shown in figures without exact plotted values in the supplied text. Deterioration rates quantify the share of models worse than their baselines, not the size of the performance change.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1–8 report aggregate GE and NT comparisons for baseline and regularized models, but the supplied text gives no exact values; not added as rows. Figures 9–12 show distributions and selected best/worst models without extractable numerical results. Table 5 profiling time is outside the claim.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test-error changes when width increases beyond zero training error; no controlled width sweep or interpolation threshold is reported.
Convolutional versus fully connected classification error on images and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets; Adam and RMSprop are search choices rather than a reported controlled comparison.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes; batch size is only a search hyperparameter.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error, small-training-set exceptions, excessive-dropout underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, training–test gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining to measure test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All 24 numerical values match Table 4. Each condition contains 200 selected baseline models, and regularizer settings are selected for best GE, breaking GE=1 ties by NT; the rates therefore describe tuned counterparts, not arbitrary regularizer settings. A zero deterioration rate permits ties and does not prove every model improves. The supplied source is the 2022 preprint identifying the 2024 publication, so these conclusions apply to the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error on image datasets.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error in the stated regimes; this study reports side-channel attack performance instead.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
